Having leaders is a really cemented idea in the human psyche. Since before we were monkeys, we have been pack animals. Note, we are not herd animals, which are different from pack animals. Humans are hunters, and because of this we have pack leaders: the most fit units for protecting and leading our social groups. These are the "alphas," and their brains are wired differently than the followers.

Some scientists will argue leaders are born, not created via circumstance. Most would probably agree though, that in modern humans alpha traits are both nature and nurture. In humans, evedence is is seen in history when great leaders cede their power to an heir, who turns out to be either completely unfit to lead, or downright evil. Their genetics are very similar to the parent, but they still mess up. Hence, nature and nurture both have a part to be played.

Things got really complicated as human population increased, and as technology made the world smaller. Rulers now govern over hundreds of millions, rather than the 1000 people you might find in an 1800's town. We still hold on to the same instinct to be lead by an "alpha," but now we chose our alphas for completely different reasons. Most people will never even see their president outside of media, and therefore have few of the original tricks we use to sense danger, and identify the best leader.

Things are enven further compunded by the fact that humans are (usually) moral, but we choose our leaders using a system that favors incompetent psychopaths over honest humanists.

In short, I think humanity has mostly outgrown the need for leaders that represent more than a few thousand people. However, psychopaths dont usually win local elections because such a great portion of their represented populous will meet them face to face, and will note all the same red flags you get from a shady car salesman. Those psychos would be almost totally irrelivant to humanity without jobs as leaders, so naturally they hold onto their power with all their will.

So if leaders are here to stay, perhaps we as a species need to invent a new way to vet our leaders. Perhaps a return to tribal-scale townships, using communism in groups of >1000, and capitalism to deal inbetween tribes. Perhaps we put a limit on how many people any one leader can represent. Maybe we as a species start to criticize mainstream media, until fox/cnn have the same credibility as a gas station tabloid.

In summary: if herd mentaility is part of the human condition, the most effective course to a better world is to limit those tools that leaders use to exploit the herd mentaility within us all.

I think one of the most fundamental problems with representative governments is when one person represents millions, as we have, you only need corrupt one individual instead of millions. There's the education argument in that most Americans ironically think other Americans are stupid, but I don't think that really holds. Look at the polls on nearly any topic and we tend to pick the 'right' answer pretty consistently. The only time we really get things wrong is when there's hardcore propaganda and lying like in the buildup for our invasion of Iraq, but even there we acknowledged pretty quickly we made a mistake and should not be there. In any case it's not like our representatives pick the most intelligent option. They, for the most part, intentionally pick the most politically favorable option.

I think a direct democracy, as insane as it may sound to many, would work. Elon Musk has actually talked about going this route for the Martian government but with some other changes. In particular laws would be short - something like 1000 words or less. Even our professional politicians don't actually read the laws they're voting on. And laws would automatically expire after some period of time and either be revoted into law or taken off the books. This would keep the law relatively simple instead of our system where we have tens of thousands of laws so complex that even lawyers tend to be experts only on small specialized segments of the law. Another thing would be requiring a large majority to pass a law, while allowing a small minority to revoke a law. The idea there is only passing laws almost everybody agrees with, but simultaneously working to prevent a tyranny of the majority.

Most of the developed world now also uses proportional representation systems which make it pretty easy to put people with any meaningful level of support into office. It's just in our outdated system where scoring second highest in votes means you get 0% of the representation whereas getting 20% of the votes can mean you get 100% of the representation so long as the #2 guy got 19%. It's pretty silly and helps keep putting representatives into office who don't really, as a whole, represent the people. So even though there are still titles and hierarchy, much of the developed world has already moved onto more 'fair' systems of politics.
